extracted.intended_audience: educated readers of literary and political criticism; readers interested in political theory and history
extracted.subtask_description: A critical essay (19th-century style) evaluating another author's political and religious arguments about government, public works, taxation, and social policy. The piece marshals historical examples and practical reasoning to test the consistency, evidence, and consequences of the targeted author's claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand for explicit proof of economic principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory of finance must be proven rather than asserted; similitudes and loose analogies (e.g., evaporation and dew) are insufficient as foundations for fiscal theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept sweeping economic claims without clear demonstration or reasoning. The reviewer explicitly challenges Mr. Southey to 'try to prove this principle' rather than rest on metaphor or assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish usefulness of expenditure by demonstrable outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Useful public expenditure should be judged by its practical results and utility, not by ostentation or the fame of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure a public work’s utility by indicators such as tolls collected, public willingness to pay, or demonstrable convenience, rather than by its architectural grandeur or the reputation of its patrons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private investment as test of public utility
rubrics_metrics.description: If private individuals will invest in a canal, bridge, or tunnel expecting profit, that connection between private motive and public utility is evidence of usefulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence (or absence) of profitable private speculation as an empirical test: works profitable to private investors generally provide public advantage; those that would never attract private funding are less likely to be genuinely useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about government superiority in spending
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not assume governments will always spend better than private individuals; the only ground for such an assumption is evidence that governments are more likely to spend on genuinely good objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proposals for state intervention by comparing likely government competence and incentives to those of private actors; beware of arguments that treat government expenditure as inherently superior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit government duties to demonstrable public purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: The magistrate’s proper business is chiefly to secure persons and property; extending government into 'jack-of-all-trades' roles (architect, schoolmaster, moral director) is suspect unless fitness and effectiveness are shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether government intervention addresses tasks for which it has particular competence; consider division of labour and whether rulers have better information or motives than those governed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness of means, not just goodness of ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a moral or political end is desirable, the suitability and consequences of the means used to pursue it must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask not only whether an end (e.g., religious training of the people) is good, but whether government is an appropriate and effective instrument to achieve it; evaluate risks of adverse consequences from chosen means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free discussion as the best means of truth formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Men are most likely to form just opinions when they discuss freely and are exempt from influence of hope or fear; government interference substitutes force, threats, or bribes for argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize open debate and contest of reasons over coercive methods. Treat governmental attempts to suppress or discipline discussion as undermining the conditions for discovering truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of paternalistic training leading to backlash
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical experiments of governments training people in religion or morals (e.g., Laud/Charles I, Puritan regimes) produced revolutions or perverse outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating proposals to 'train' a people by state power, consider historical precedents showing that enforced conformity often breeds hypocrisy, resentment, or eventual collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question premises that religion is the necessary basis of government
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that 'religion is the basis upon which civil government rests' is challenged: government can have temporal bases and existed without religious sanction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize arguments that make religion the foundational justification for civil institutions; seek historical and logical support rather than accepting sweeping axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for internal consistency in an author's system
rubrics_metrics.description: An author's positions must be checked for contradictions (e.g., 'a people may be too rich, but a government cannot be so'), and inconsistent reasoning should undermine confidence in their system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and expose self-contradictions; do not allow eloquent phrasing to hide incompatible premises or conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure danger and stability by latent discontent, not surface conformity
rubrics_metrics.description: The security of a state is better judged by what stays in the public mind (hidden discontent) rather than by outward demonstrations of obedience or manufactured unanimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate political stability by looking for suppressed resentments and private attitudes, not merely public conformity or absence of open dissent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use empirical historical evidence to test nostalgic claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Romanticized comparisons with the past (e.g., asserting people were happier or better fed in an earlier century) must be tested against records and data (household books, contemporary accounts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand concrete evidence when authors idealize historical eras; consult primary sources and material indicators (food, lodging, medical care) before accepting claims of past superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assuming rulers are naturally wiser or better than the governed
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no general guarantee that magistrates or rulers will form just opinions more reliably than the people; methods of appointment (birth, lot, election) do not secure superior wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require positive reasons or evidence before accepting claims that a class or office-holder is more likely to be right than the general populace; question proposals that rely on such assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemn intolerance and persecution as politically and morally dangerous
rubrics_metrics.description: Excluding or persecuting dissenting religious or intellectual views (or groups) is criticized as both inconsistent and likely to produce serious social harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess policies towards dissent by their moral costs and likely political repercussions; recognize that past persecutions often produced corruption, hypocrisy, or social ruin.
